claim: 169 heterozygous diploid Saccharomyces cerevisiae mutation accumulation lines were generated across nine genetic backgrounds.
source: To characterize the genome-wide landscape and dynamics of LOH accumulation, we generated 180 MA lines using nine different heterozygous S. cerevisiae strains (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of MA lines and genetic backgrounds used in the study.

claim: The diploid hybrids were designed to have heterozygosity levels ranging from 0.1% to 1%.
source: These hybrids were designed to lead to a heterozygosity level ranging from 0.1% to 1%, covering a large genetic diversity of the S. cerevisiae species.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the range of heterozygosity levels in the designed hybrids.

claim: A total of 22,828 LOH events were detected across the 169 MA lines.
source: Overall, we identified a large set of 22,828 LOH events across the 169 MA lines, with an average size of 14.1 kb (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the total number of LOH events detected.

claim: The average size of LOH events is 14.1 kb.
source: Overall, we identified a large set of 22,828 LOH events across the 169 MA lines, with an average size of 14.1 kb (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the average size of LOH events.

claim: The size distribution of LOH events is bimodal.
source: It is interesting to observe that the size distribution of the detected LOH events is bimodal (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the bimodal distribution and references Figure 1A showing this distribution.

claim: 95% of LOH events have an average size of 1.6 kb.
source: While the majority of the events (95%) are in the first category with an average size of 1.6 kb, the rest of the events (5%) in the second category have an average size of 269.2 kb.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the percentage and average size for the first category of LOH events.

claim: 5% of LOH events have an average size of 269.2 kb.
source: While the majority of the events (95%) are in the first category with an average size of 1.6 kb, the rest of the events (5%) in the second category have an average size of 269.2 kb.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the percentage and average size for the second category of LOH events.

claim: Interstitial LOH (I-LOH) events represent 86.1% of all LOH events (n = 19,660).
source: Among the accumulated events, the I-LOHs were found to be significantly enriched representing 86.1% of the events (n = 19,660) compared to the T-LOHs with only 3,168 detected events (i.e. 13.9%) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage and count of I-LOH events.

claim: Terminal LOH (T-LOH) events represent 13.9% of all LOH events (n = 3,168).
source: Among the accumulated events, the I-LOHs were found to be significantly enriched representing 86.1% of the events (n = 19,660) compared to the T-LOHs with only 3,168 detected events (i.e. 13.9%) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage and count of T-LOH events.

claim: T-LOH events are significantly larger than I-LOH events with average sizes of 55.3 kb and 7.5 kb, respectively.
source: As expected, T-LOH events are significantly larger than I-LOH events with an average size of 55.3 and 7.5 kb, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, p<10−3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the sizes of T-LOH and I-LOH events with statistical significance.

claim: On average, 15.9% of the genome was under LOH across the 169 MA lines.
source: On average, 15.9% of the genome was under LOH but with a large variation as this fraction ranges from 0.01% to 98.6% across the lines.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the average percentage of genome under LOH.

claim: The fraction of genome under LOH ranges from 0.01% to 98.6% across the lines.
source: On average, 15.9% of the genome was under LOH but with a large variation as this fraction ranges from 0.01% to 98.6% across the lines.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the range of genome under LOH.

claim: 14 lines exhibited more than 90% of the genome under LOH and are designated as nearly homozygous lines.
source: The last group encompassed 14 lines that exhibit more than 90% of the genome under LOH, which is significantly higher than the other two (Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5). This observation clearly shows that the genome of approximately 8% of the lines was quickly driven a quasi-homozygous state, henceforth we call them nearly homozygous lines.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies and names the nearly homozygous lines.

claim: The LOH rate is 7.1 × 10−5 per site per division on average.
source: Using the 169 lines, we estimated the LOH rates to be 7.1 × 10−5 per site per division and 6.5 × 10−2 events per division on average.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the LOH rate per site per division.

claim: The LOH rate is 6.5 × 10−2 events per division on average.
source: Using the 169 lines, we estimated the LOH rates to be 7.1 × 10−5 per site per division and 6.5 × 10−2 events per division on average.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the LOH rate per division.

claim: The I-LOH rate is 3.1 × 10−5 per site per division.
source: While the I-LOH rates were 3.1 × 10−5 per site per division and 5.6 × 10−2 events per division, we found that the T-LOH rates were 4.2 × 10−5 per site per division and 9.2 × 10−3 events per division.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the I-LOH rate per site per division.

claim: The I-LOH rate is 5.6 × 10−2 events per division.
source: While the I-LOH rates were 3.1 × 10−5 per site per division and 5.6 × 10−2 events per division, we found that the T-LOH rates were 4.2 × 10−5 per site per division and 9.2 × 10−3 events per division.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the I-LOH rate per division.

claim: The T-LOH rate is 4.2 × 10−5 per site per division.
source: While the I-LOH rates were 3.1 × 10−5 per site per division and 5.6 × 10−2 events per division, we found that the T-LOH rates were 4.2 × 10−5 per site per division and 9.2 × 10−3 events per division.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the T-LOH rate per site per division.

claim: The T-LOH rate is 9.2 × 10−3 events per division.
source: While the I-LOH rates were 3.1 × 10−5 per site per division and 5.6 × 10−2 events per division, we found that the T-LOH rates were 4.2 × 10−5 per site per division and 9.2 × 10−3 events per division.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the T-LOH rate per division.

claim: The number of accumulated LOH events varies considerably between genetic backgrounds, with H1 lines accumulating the fewest (n = 10.8 on average) and H4 lines accumulating the most (n = 413.5 on average), representing a 38.2-fold difference.
source: While the H1 lines accumulated the fewest LOH events (n = 10.8 on average), the H4 lines accumulated the largest number of events (n = 413.5 on average), which represents a difference of 38.2 times.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the LOH event counts between different genetic backgrounds.

claim: I-LOH events are significantly in excess compared to T-LOH events in most genetic backgrounds (except for H1 and H9 lines).
source: In most cases (except for the H1 and H9 lines), the I-LOH events were significantly in excess compared to T-LOH events in all backgrounds (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the predominance of I-LOH events in most backgrounds with exceptions.

claim: There is a positive correlation between heterozygosity level and the number of T-LOH events.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the more the ancestors were heterozygous, the more they accumulated T-LOH events (Figure 2B). And we have indeed found a positive correlation between the heterozygosity level and the number of T-LOH events (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes and shows a positive correlation between heterozygosity and T-LOH events.

claim: No correlation was found between heterozygosity level and I-LOH events or total LOH events.
source: Such a correlation was found neither for I-LOH nor for the total number of LOH events accumulated in the lines.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of correlation for I-LOH and total LOH events.

claim: The proportion of genome under LOH varies from 3.6% to 16.6% across the nine backgrounds (excluding nearly homozygous lines).
source: This fraction varies from 3.6% to 16.6% of the genome across the nine backgrounds, when we exclude the nearly homozygous lines reaching more than 90% of the genome being under LOH (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the range of genome under LOH across backgrounds.

claim: H3 lines accumulated the most genome under LOH (16.6%) while H8 accumulated the least (3.8%), representing a 4.6-fold difference.
source: The H3 lines accumulated the most genome under LOH (16.6%) while H8 accumulated the least (3.8%), representing a 4.6-fold difference.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the genome under LOH between H3 and H8 backgrounds.

claim: The H9 background was enriched in nearly homozygous lines (n = 5), while H1 and H4 had none.
source: In addition, the H9 background was enriched in nearly homozygous lines (n = 5), while H1 and H4 had none (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the distribution of nearly homozygous lines across backgrounds.

claim: Biased fixation toward one parent was observed only in H4 and H5 backgrounds.
source: We did not observe a significant excess in fixation of either of the parental genomes in the different backgrounds (binomial test, p>0.05), except for the H4 and H5 lines (binomial test, p<0.05).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies H4 and H5 as showing biased fixation with statistical testing.

claim: In H4 and H5 backgrounds, more than 80% of the genome under LOH is biased toward one of the parents.
source: In both, H4 and H5, more than 80% of the genome under LOH is biased toward one of the parents (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), although the total genome under LOH in these backgrounds was very low with a level of 5.5% and 4.8%, respectively.

claim: LOH site rates vary between 2.4 × 10−5 and 1.1 × 10−4 per site per division across the nine hybrids.
source: The LOH site rates in these hybrids vary between 2.4 × 10−5 and 1.1 × 10−4 per site per division, and consequently a low variance was observed (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the range of LOH site rates.

claim: LOH event rates range from 5.6 × 10−3 to 2.8 × 10−1 events per division and are much more variable than site rates.
source: By contrast, the LOH event rates range from 5.6 × 10−3 to 2.8 × 10−1 events per division and are hence much more variable.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the range of LOH event rates and notes their variability.

claim: Spore viability in the ancestral diploids varies between 38% and 92%.
source: By determining the spore viability as a measure of spore fertility in the ancestors, we indeed saw that it varies between 38% and 92% (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the range of spore viability in ancestors.

claim: H1, H2, H3, H6, and H7 ancestors displayed good spore fertility (~85%).
source: While the H1, H2, H3, H6, and H7 ancestors displayed good spore fertility (~85%), the spore viability of the H4, H5, H8, and H9 ancestors was severely compromised (~50%) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly categorizes ancestors by spore fertility levels.

claim: The spore viability of H4, H5, H8, and H9 ancestors was severely compromised (~50%).
source: While the H1, H2, H3, H6, and H7 ancestors displayed good spore fertility (~85%), the spore viability of the H4, H5, H8, and H9 ancestors was severely compromised (~50%) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly categorizes ancestors by spore fertility levels.

claim: Lines with high spore fertility accumulated much less LOH events than lines with low spore fertility, with a 7.6-fold higher frequency in low fertility lines.
source: Interestingly, we observed that lines with high spore fertility accumulated much less LOH events than the lines showing low spore fertility (Figure 3A). The frequency in these was 7.6-fold higher per bottleneck.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares LOH accumulation between high and low fertility lines.

claim: The size of LOH events was on average much shorter in low spore fertility lines.
source: In addition, we also found that the size of the LOH events was on average much shorter in low spore fertility lines (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the difference in LOH event size between fertility groups.

claim: In lines with high spore fertility, I-LOH events were three times more frequent than T-LOH events.
source: In lines with high spore fertility, I-LOH events were three times more frequent than those of T-LOH, similar to what had previously been observed in the W303/YJM789 hybrid (Sui et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the ratio of I-LOH to T-LOH in high fertility lines and cites supporting literature.

claim: In low spore fertility hybrids, I-LOH events were seven-fold more frequent than T-LOH events.
source: However, I-LOH events were even more frequent (seven-fold) than T-LOH in the low spore fertility hybrids with low spore fertility.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the ratio of I-LOH to T-LOH in low fertility lines.

claim: The mean LOH event size in high spore fertility lines is 45.8 kb compared to 7.4 kb in low spore fertility hybrids.
source: The mean LOH event size in the latter is 45.8 kb compared to 7.4 kb in low spore fertility hybrids.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares mean LOH event sizes between fertility groups.

claim: MA lines derived from low spore fertility ancestors showed significant improvement in spore viability compared to their ancestors.
source: By contrast, individual lines of the four other backgrounds presenting a low spore fertility (lines H4, H5, H8, and H9) showed significant increase compared to the ancestral spore fertility (Figure 3C).

claim: The spore viability of lines derived from highly fertile hybrids did not deviate significantly from their ancestral levels.
source: The spore viability of the lines derived from the highly fertile hybrids did not deviate significantly from their ancestral levels, meaning that they retained their high spore viability.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that high fertility lines maintained their spore viability.

source: Rescue of the spore fertility in most MA lines was gradual, with only 42 out of 77 lines showing statistically significant increases (Supplementary file 4).

claim: MA lines showed up to a 23% increase in spore fertility.
source: MA lines showed up to a 23% increase in spore fertility and the nearly homozygous lines from all hybrid backgrounds were able to fully restore their spore fertility (~90%).

claim: Nearly homozygous lines from all hybrid backgrounds were able to fully restore their spore fertility (~90%).
source: MA lines showed up to a 23% increase in spore fertility and the nearly homozygous lines from all hybrid backgrounds were able to fully restore their spore fertility (~90%).

S. cerevisiae is highly inbred and characterized by irregular sexual cycles (Ruderfer et al., 2006). Meiosis and consequently outcrossing events are infrequent, and the clonal expansion is punctuated by a broad LOH accumulation. As a consequence, a high LOH level with 25 regions covering approximately 50% of the genome on average was observed in this large panel (Peter et al., 2018).
